learningObjectives: Identify the soma, fine perisynaptic processes, vascular endfeet, gap-junction network and principal transporter systems of an astrocyte.
Explain how astrocytes stabilise extracellular potassium and clear glutamate after synaptic activity.
Describe the tripartite synapse and the astrocyte contribution to metabolic and neurovascular support.
Apply astrocyte principles to seizures, excitotoxicity, blood–brain barrier dysfunction and reactive astrogliosis without treating glia as passive support cells.

anatomy.label: Astrocyte soma
anatomy.detail: The soma contains the nucleus and biosynthetic machinery that maintain the astrocyte's extensive territorial processes. A single astrocyte can coordinate local homeostasis across many synapses.
anatomy.clinical: Astrocytes are metabolically active cells, not inert packing material. Their failure can alter neuronal function even when neurons remain structurally intact.

anatomy.label: Perisynaptic processes
anatomy.detail: Very fine astrocytic processes approach or envelop synapses. They sense transmitter release, shape extracellular chemistry and help limit spillover between neighbouring synapses.
anatomy.clinical: The tripartite synapse frames transmission as an interaction among the presynaptic neuron, postsynaptic neuron and nearby astrocyte.

anatomy.label: Glutamate transporters
anatomy.detail: Astrocytic excitatory amino-acid transporters, especially EAAT2 in humans, remove much of the glutamate released into the extracellular space. Astrocytes then convert glutamate to glutamine for reuse by neurons.
anatomy.clinical: Impaired glutamate clearance can increase excitotoxic stress and destabilise networks. This is clinically relevant to epilepsy, injury and several neurodegenerative conditions.

anatomy.label: Potassium buffering
anatomy.detail: Neuronal firing raises extracellular potassium. Astrocytes take up and redistribute potassium through channels and coupled networks, helping preserve the gradients required for reliable excitability.
anatomy.clinical: Failure of potassium homeostasis can lower seizure threshold and amplify pathological synchrony.

anatomy.label: Vascular endfeet
anatomy.detail: Astrocytic endfeet closely cover cerebral microvessels. They participate in the neurovascular unit, support barrier properties and help match local perfusion to neural activity.
anatomy.clinical: Functional imaging relies on neurovascular coupling. BOLD signal is therefore an indirect haemodynamic correlate of neural activity, shaped by neuron–glia–vascular interactions.

anatomy.label: Metabolic support
anatomy.detail: Astrocytes store glycogen, process glucose and provide metabolic substrates that support active neurons. Their position between synapses and blood vessels makes them key coordinators of local energy demand.
anatomy.clinical: Sleep loss, hypoxia and metabolic stress can impair cognition partly by disturbing the systems that support neuronal energy use.

anatomy.label: Gap-junction network
anatomy.detail: Astrocytes connect to neighbouring astrocytes through gap junctions, allowing ions and small molecules to redistribute across a functional network rather than remaining confined to one cell.
anatomy.clinical: Homeostasis is distributed. A local disturbance may be buffered across an astrocytic network, but widespread dysfunction can reduce that reserve.

interaction.instruction: Select an astrocyte system, then run the support cycle to follow glutamate clearance, potassium buffering and blood-flow matching.
supportSteps: Synaptic activity releases glutamate and raises extracellular potassium.
Perisynaptic astrocyte processes detect and take up these signals.
Glutamate is converted to glutamine and returned to neurons for transmitter synthesis.
Potassium is redistributed through astrocytic channels and gap-junction networks.
Vascular endfeet help coordinate local blood flow and metabolic support with tissue demand.

quizBank.question: Which astrocyte function most directly limits glutamate accumulation outside neurons?
options: EAAT-mediated uptake
Myelin wrapping
Microglial phagocytosis
Axonal sodium influx
quizBank.explanation: Astrocytic excitatory amino-acid transporters rapidly clear extracellular glutamate and help prevent spillover and excitotoxic stress.

quizBank.question: What does the tripartite synapse add to the traditional two-neuron model?
options: A nearby astrocyte that senses and regulates synaptic activity
A second axon hillock
A vascular smooth-muscle cell inside the cleft
A microglial nucleus in the postsynaptic neuron
quizBank.explanation: The tripartite concept recognises the perisynaptic astrocyte as an active participant alongside pre- and postsynaptic neuronal elements.

quizBank.question: Why is astrocytic potassium buffering important?
options: It stabilises neuronal excitability after firing
It generates action potentials in myelin
It converts dopamine into serotonin
It creates cerebrospinal fluid in ventricles
quizBank.explanation: Neuronal activity raises extracellular potassium; astrocytes help redistribute it so membrane gradients and network stability are maintained.

quizBank.question: Astrocytic vascular endfeet are part of which functional system?
options: The neurovascular unit
The corticospinal tract
The ventricular choroid plexus only
The peripheral neuromuscular junction
quizBank.explanation: Endfeet contact cerebral microvessels and contribute to barrier support, metabolic exchange and activity-linked blood-flow regulation.

quizBank.question: Which statement about reactive astrogliosis is most accurate?
options: It can be protective or maladaptive depending on context and duration
It always means astrocytes have died
It is identical to bacterial meningitis
It has no effect on neuronal networks
quizBank.explanation: Reactive astrocyte responses are heterogeneous. They may contain injury and restore homeostasis, but persistent or dysregulated responses can also impede recovery.

reviewPrompts: Name three homeostatic functions performed by astrocytes.
Explain the tripartite synapse in one sentence.
Trace glutamate from synaptic release to neuronal reuse.
Explain why potassium buffering matters for seizure threshold.
Distinguish adaptive from potentially maladaptive reactive astrogliosis.
